910.name: Pannonia & the Migrations Era
910.description: The Carpathian Basin was the Roman province of Pannonia, then a migration corridor for Huns, Gepids, Avars, and Slavic peoples. The Avar Khaganate dominated for 250 years before Frankish and Slavic successor polities emerged.

sub_clusters.name: Roman Pannonia
sub_clusters.description: The Roman province of Pannonia, with Aquincum (Budapest) as its capital, served as a crucial Danubian frontier (limes). Significant Roman urban and military infrastructure, Christianity's early spread, and the Hunnic invasion under Attila.

sub_clusters.name: Avars & Pre-Magyar Period
sub_clusters.description: The Hunnic Empire, Gepid Kingdom, Avar Khaganate (567–803), and Slavic settlement. Charlemagne's destruction of the Avar ring fortress (796) and the brief Slavic Principality of Balaton preceded the Magyar arrival.

920.name: Magyar Conquest & Árpád Kingdom
920.description: The Magyar conquest of the Carpathian Basin (honfoglalás, 895/896) under Árpád founded the Hungarian state. St. Stephen I's Christianisation (1000), the Mongol invasion (1241), and the extinction of the Árpád dynasty (1301) shaped medieval Hungary.

sub_clusters.name: Magyar Conquest & Western Raids
sub_clusters.description: Árpád's conquest of the Carpathian Basin, Magyar raids terrifying Western Europe from Italy to Spain, and the decisive defeat at the Battle of Lechfeld (955) by Otto I, ending the raiding era.
key_events: Magyar conquest of the Carpathian Basin (honfoglalás, 895/896)

sub_clusters.name: St. Stephen & the Christian Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: Stephen I's coronation (Christmas Day 1000/January 1, 1001) with a crown from Pope Sylvester II established Christian Hungary. The Admonitions to his son, county system, and integration into medieval Christendom.
key_events: Coronation of St. Stephen I — founding of the Kingdom of Hungary (1000/1001)

sub_clusters.name: Mongol Invasion & Late Árpáds
sub_clusters.description: The Golden Bull (1222, Hungary's 'Magna Carta'), the catastrophic Mongol invasion (1241–42) that killed up to half the population, Béla IV's reconstruction with stone castles, and the extinction of the Árpád dynasty (1301).

920.name: Angevin & Late Medieval Hungary
920.description: The Angevin dynasty and Matthias Corvinus brought Hungary to its peak of medieval power. Hungary became Central Europe's wealthiest kingdom under Charles I's gold-based economy and Matthias's Renaissance court.

sub_clusters.name: Angevin Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Charles I Robert's gold currency reform and Louis the Great's expansion — Hungary became the largest gold producer in Europe. The Personal Union with Poland (1370–1382) extended Hungarian influence.

sub_clusters.name: Hunyadi & Matthias Corvinus
sub_clusters.description: John Hunyadi's defence against Ottoman expansion, the victory at Belgrade (1456). Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490) created a Renaissance court, the Bibliotheca Corviniana, and briefly controlled Vienna and Bohemia.
key_events: Siege of Belgrade — Hunyadi defeats Ottoman army (1456)

930.name: Ottoman Occupation & Habsburg Reconquest
930.description: The catastrophic defeat at Mohács (1526) led to 150 years of Ottoman occupation of central Hungary. The kingdom was tripartite-divided between Ottomans, Habsburgs, and the Transylvanian Principality, until Habsburg reconquest in the 1680s–90s.

sub_clusters.name: Battle of Mohács & Tripartite Partition
sub_clusters.description: The disastrous Battle of Mohács (August 29, 1526), where King Louis II was killed, led to Ottoman conquest of Buda (1541) and Hungary's division into three parts: Ottoman Hungary, Royal (Habsburg) Hungary, and the Principality of Transylvania.
key_events: Battle of Mohács (August 29, 1526) — Hungarian state destroyed

sub_clusters.name: Ottoman Hungary & Habsburg Reconquest
sub_clusters.description: 150 years of Ottoman rule over central Hungary: Turkish baths in Buda, population decline, and continuous frontier warfare. The Great Turkish War (1683–99), the Siege of Buda (1686), and the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) restored Habsburg control.

940.name: Habsburg Rule & National Awakening
940.description: Habsburg absolutism provoked Rákóczi's War of Independence (1703–1711). The Hungarian Reform Era, the 1848 Revolution under Kossuth, and the brutal Austrian repression that followed reshaped Hungarian national consciousness.

sub_clusters.name: Rákóczi Uprising & Habsburg Absolutism
sub_clusters.description: Francis II Rákóczi's War of Independence (1703–1711) against Habsburg absolutism, the Peace of Szatmár, and the era of Habsburg centralisation, colonisation, and Maria Theresa's and Joseph II's reforms.

sub_clusters.name: Reform Era & 1848 Revolution
sub_clusters.description: Count István Széchenyi's modernisation programme, Lajos Kossuth's revolutionary agitation, the 1848 Revolution and War of Independence, Russian intervention, and the Austrian military repression (Haynau's executions at Arad).
key_events: Hungarian Revolution of 1848 — Kossuth declares independence
Execution of the 13 Martyrs of Arad (October 6, 1849)

940.name: Austro-Hungarian Compromise & Dual Monarchy
940.description: The Ausgleich (Compromise) of 1867 created the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary, granting Hungary internal autonomy. Rapid industrialisation, Budapest's golden age, ethnic tensions with national minorities, and the catastrophe of WWI.

sub_clusters.name: Dual Monarchy & Budapest's Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: The Compromise gave Hungary self-government. Budapest was unified (1873), the Hungarian Parliament building constructed, the Millennium celebrations (1896), and rapid industrial and cultural development made Budapest a major European capital.

sub_clusters.name: Nationalities Crisis & WWI
sub_clusters.description: Growing tensions with Slavic, Romanian, and other minorities. Hungary entered WWI as part of the Central Powers, suffering enormous casualties. The collapse of the Dual Monarchy and the armistice (November 1918) ended the old order.

950.name: Trianon, Interwar Period & WWII
950.description: The Treaty of Trianon (1920) stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its territory and one-third of ethnic Hungarians. Irredentist revisionism dominated the Horthy era. Alliance with Nazi Germany brought temporary gains but ended in catastrophic defeat and the Holocaust.

sub_clusters.name: Treaty of Trianon & Horthy Era
sub_clusters.description: The brief Soviet Republic under Béla Kun (1919), Miklós Horthy's authoritarian regency, the Treaty of Trianon (June 4, 1920) — the defining trauma of modern Hungarian history — and the Vienna Awards (1938, 1940) recovering Slovak and Transylvanian territories.
key_events: Treaty of Trianon (June 4, 1920) — Hungary loses 2/3 of territory

sub_clusters.name: WWII & the Holocaust in Hungary
sub_clusters.description: Hungary's entry into WWII alongside the Axis, the disastrous Second Army destruction at the Don (1943), Arrow Cross takeover (October 1944), the deportation and murder of 565,000 Hungarian Jews, and the devastating Siege of Budapest (1944–45).

950.name: Communist Era & 1956 Uprising
950.description: Soviet-imposed communist rule, Rákosi's Stalinist terror, the heroic 1956 Hungarian Uprising crushed by Soviet tanks, Kádár's subsequent 'goulash communism' allowing limited economic liberalisation, and the gradual opening that preceded the 1989 transition.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinist Era & 1956 Uprising
sub_clusters.description: Communist takeover through 'salami tactics', Rákosi's Stalinist terror (Rajk trial), and the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 — a heroic but doomed uprising crushed by Soviet military intervention, with Imre Nagy executed (1958).
key_events: Hungarian Revolution of 1956 — crushed by Soviet tanks

sub_clusters.name: Kádár Era: Goulash Communism
sub_clusters.description: János Kádár's pragmatic rule: the New Economic Mechanism (1968), relative consumerism ('the happiest barracks in the camp'), cautious cultural liberalisation, and the gradual economic opening that made Hungary the first Eastern Bloc country to open its borders (1989).

960.name: Democratic Transition & Contemporary Hungary
960.description: Hungary's peaceful transition (1989), EU and NATO accession, and the rise of Viktor Orbán's Fidesz government with its 'illiberal democracy' model challenging European norms.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Transition & EU Integration
sub_clusters.description: The Pan-European Picnic (August 1989) and border opening, peaceful transition, NATO membership (1999), EU accession (2004), and the painful economic transition including the 2006 political crisis and 2008 financial crisis.

sub_clusters.name: Orbán Era & Illiberal Turn
sub_clusters.description: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz supermajority (2010), the 2011 Fundamental Law, media consolidation, anti-immigration stance (2015 border fence), 'illiberal democracy' rhetoric, EU rule-of-law clashes, and Hungary's ambiguous position during the Ukraine crisis.
